But when I look at the timestamps, and there are missing attachments, and then certain community members kind of avoid answering my questions… it just seems obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened.\n\nI don’t want to sound unreasonable. I just… I need help figuring out how to deal with it, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe for certain that people are hiding the truth about your father’s death?\n\nPatient: I mean… “for certain” sounds so strong, and I don’t want to come across like I’m refusing to consider anything else. But yes, when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and then the way some people in the community avoid answering me directly, it really does feel obvious to me that someone is hiding what actually happened around my father’s death.\n\nI know that may sound like I’m reading too much into it, but I can’t honestly say I believe the official explanation.\n\nDoctor: Outside of what happened with your father’s death, do you often feel that other people are hiding things from you or trying to deceive you?\n\nPatient: No, not really in a general way. I don’t walk around thinking everyone is deceiving me or anything like that.\n\nIt’s more… this specific situation with my father. I know people keep saying the hospital records and the donation emails line up, and maybe I sound stuck on it, but when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and how certain people in the community avoid my questions, it feels pretty obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened. I’m not trying to make it bigger than it is. That’s just the part I can’t get past.\n\nDoctor: If clear proof showed that nothing was being hidden about your father’s death, would you be able to accept it?\n\nPatient: I’d like to say yes, because I know that’s probably the reasonable answer. If it was truly clear proof… I mean, I would try to accept it.\n\nBut honestly, I think I’d still have trouble, because everyone keeps saying the hospital records and donation emails line up, and yet when I look at the timestamps, the missing attachments, and how certain people avoid answering my questions, it just still seems obvious to me that something is being hidden about what really happened. I know that may not be the answer you’re looking for, but that’s where I get stuck.\n\nDoctor: How long have you believed that something is being hidden about your father’s death?\n\nPatient: It’s been… about nine months, I think. Not years or anything like that.\n\nIt really started after my father died, when I was going through his records and messages. That’s when I started noticing things that didn’t seem right to me. It kind of built up as I was sorting through everything.\n\nDoctor: Since your father died, have you been feeling a strong, persistent longing or yearning for him?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d call it strong or persistent, exactly. I mean, of course I miss him—he was my father. I don’t want to make it sound more dramatic than it is.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone else told you they agree that something is being hidden about your father’s death?\n\nPatient: Not really… I mean, a few people have said they understand why I’m asking questions, but I don’t think anyone has flat-out said, “Yes, you’re right, something is being hidden.”\n\nMost people keep telling me the hospital records and the donation emails line up. I know that may not be the answer you want, but that’s honestly how it feels.\n\nDoctor: When other people show you evidence that your father’s death was not being covered up, do you still believe a cover-up happened?\n\nPatient: I try to listen when people show me things, I really do. It’s just where my mind goes, even when I’m trying not to focus on it.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think you might be mistaken about this, and that the feeling of a cover-up could be coming from your own mind rather than from something actually being hidden?\n\nPatient: I mean… I’ve tried to consider that. I just… I can’t honestly say I think I’m mistaken.\n\nDoctor: Do these thoughts about a cover-up feel unwanted and intrusive to you?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d call them unwanted in the way you mean. I don’t enjoy thinking about it, obviously, and I’d rather things just made sense so I could leave it alone.\n\nBut it’s not like some random thought popping in for no reason.
